You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I borrowed my friend's tripod, and I can't seem to find the part that connects the camera to the tripod. How hard would it be to 3D print it, both the flat part and the part that screws in? Just as a temporary thing until I find the real one. I know it's metal normally.
I'll take a few measurements first. The plate has to match your friend's tripod head, and a ready-made metal bolt will hold much better than a printed screw thread.
reasoning:
Printing a 1/4-20 screw in PLA would be weak, so using the salvaged webcam-mount bolt as the camera screw makes more sense, paired with the ASME 1/4-20 nut. I still need to pin down the tripod's quick-release clamp geometry — the clamp type, likely Arca-Swiss style — before designing the plate.

With only 8 turns available, I should batch my measurement questions: clamp opening width, plate thickness the clamp grips, recess length, and dovetail/bevel angle, plus the webcam bolt's length under head, head diameter, and head height. I'll ask for all of these together.

reasoning:
Without exact measurements, this looks like a standard Arca-Swiss style plate: roughly 38 mm wide with 45° dovetail angled sides and about 4-5 mm bevel depth, fitting into knob-tightened jaws with angled lips.

I'll settle on a simplified trapezoid profile: 38mm wide base with 45° bevels narrowing to about 30mm, keeping the clamp lip engagement around 34mm to match typical Arca clamp dimensions.

I should also check print orientation so the bevels taper inward without needing supports, and I need to account for the camera bolt length and head clearance under the plate.

Settling on a 5mm floor giving 5mm bolt protrusion, with the counterbore sized to fit the head flush at 5mm deep and 16mm diameter. I'm also considering swapping the hole for a slot so the camera position stays adjustable, sizing it around 6.8mm wide by 20mm long with a matching counterbore slot.

I'll make the slot length 12mm of travel, skip the anti-twist rubber pad as just a note, and set the plate length to 60mm. I'm also planning a short 15mm test coupon slice of the profile to check the clamp fit before committing to the full part.

Printing the screw itself would be too weak in PLA, so I'll stick with a standard webcam bolt and size the clearance hole for 1/4" at 6.8mm. I'm now working out the CadQuery geometry—extruding the profile along Y, centering it, then cutting the slot with slot2D and adding a counterbore for the bolt head, figuring out how the slot orientation should run along the plate's length for Arca-compatibility.

Checking the top width against counterbore clearance—30mm top with a 16mm counterbore fits fine, floor thickness of 5mm works with a 10mm plate and 5mm counterbore depth plus head clearance. For the coupon piece I'll reuse the same cross-section profile but shorter, around 15mm, with no holes, just a coupon_len parameter.

I'm uncertain about exact Arca-swiss dimensions—the lip overhang depth and dovetail bevel contact matter but aren't fully specified, so the coupon test should help verify fit. I'll also suggest adding rubber or tape on top for anti-slip, then finalize the submission.
